items.q: Write the expression for the test statistic <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>, with the values substituted, then give its value to two decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is the standard error of an interval. A test assumes <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_0</annotation></semantics></math>, so its standard error uses the pooled proportion <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0.72</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_c = 0.72</annotation></semantics></math> for both groups.

That treats the 300 households as one sample. The standard error has a term for each group: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>160</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>140</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{160} + \frac{1}{140}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The square root is missing: that divides by the variance instead of the standard error.

items.q: What is the p-value of the test? Give four decimal places.

mistakes.why: That doubles the tail area, as for a two-sided test. Here <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a</annotation></semantics></math> is one-sided (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>></mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">></annotation></semantics></math>), so the p-value is the area to the right of <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> alone.

That is the area to the left of <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>. For <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>O</mi></msub><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a: p_N - p_O > 0</annotation></semantics></math> the p-value is the area to the right.

items.q: State the conclusion of the test in context.

options: There is convincing evidence that
There is not convincing evidence that
This proves that

why.2: A test never proves; it gives evidence.

options: is greater than
is different from
is less than

why.1: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a</annotation></semantics></math> is one-sided, so the conclusion names its direction.
why.2: The alternative is that the new bin is better.

options: the true proportion of households like these that sort correctly with the new bin ... with the old bin
the proportion of the 160 study households with new bins that sorted correctly ... with old bins
the pooled proportion of households that sort correctly ... 0.72

why.1: That describes the sample, which we know. Conclusions are about the true proportions.
why.2: The pooled proportion is a step in the calculation, not the parameter.

options: Because 0.0058 < 0.05, reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.0058 > 0.05, fail to reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.0058 > 0.05, reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.0058 < 0.05, accept the null hypothesis.

why.1: Check the inequality: the p-value 0.0058 is less than alpha 0.05, so reject the null hypothesis.
why.2: Reject only when the p-value is less than alpha.
why.3: A test never accepts the null hypothesis; it can only fail to reject it.

conclude.model: Because the p-value of 0.0058 is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of all households like these that sort their recycling correctly is greater with the new bin than with the old bin.

options: There is not convincing evidence that

options: the true proportions of likely voters who support the bond differ between the two districts
the sample proportions, 0.53 and 0.475, differ
the true proportions of likely voters who support the bond are equal in the two districts

why.1: We know the sample proportions differ. The question is about the populations.
why.2: The conclusion is stated about <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_a</annotation></semantics></math>, the claim we looked for evidence of.

options: Because 0.13 > 0.05, fail to reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.13 < 0.05, reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.13 > 0.05, reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.13 < 0.05, accept the null hypothesis.

why.1: Check the inequality: the p-value 0.13 is greater than alpha 0.05, so fail to reject the null hypothesis.
why.2: Reject only when the p-value is less than alpha.
why.3: A test never accepts the null hypothesis; it can only fail to reject it.

conclude.model: Because the p-value of 0.130 is greater than 0.05, we fail to reject the null hypothesis. There is not convincing evidence that the true proportions of all likely voters who support the park bond differ between District A and District B.

Failing to reject is not evidence of no difference

mistakes.why: That is one tail only. The alternative is two-sided (<math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>≠</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ne</annotation></semantics></math>), so double the tail area.

That is the area between the two tails. The p-value is the area in both tails beyond <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Why does a two-sample z test use <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{p_c(1 - p_c)\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}</annotation></semantics></math> while the interval uses <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">^</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}</annotation></semantics></math>?
options: The test needs a larger standard error to be fair
The interval assumes the proportions are equal
Intervals are for experiments and tests are for samples

That divides 200 equally over four cells. Use the totals: 80 work from home and 72 own a pet.

items.q: Which study calls for a chi-square test for independence rather than homogeneity?
options: Patients randomly assigned to three treatments, with the outcome recorded as better, same or worse
One random sample of 500 voters, each classified by party and by view on a ballot measure

items.q: What is the value of the chi-square statistic? Give two decimal places.

mistakes.why: That adds the squared gaps <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(O - E)^2</annotation></semantics></math> without dividing each by its expected count <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math>.

The gaps must be squared: each term is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>O</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>E</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mi>E</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{(O - E)^2}{E}</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: How many degrees of freedom does the test have?

mistakes.why: That is the number of cells minus 1. For a two-way table, <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>df</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{df}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>rows</mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>columns</mtext><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= (\text{rows} - 1)(\text{columns} - 1)</annotation></semantics></math>.

That is <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n - 1</annotation></semantics></math>. For chi-square, df depends on the table's size: <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(2 - 1)(3 - 1) = 2</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: What is the p-value? Give four decimal places.

mistakes.why: That uses 5 degrees of freedom. The table has 2 rows and 3 columns, so <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>df</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{df} = 2</annotation></semantics></math>.

That is the area to the left. A chi-square p-value is the area to the right of <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>χ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\chi^2</annotation></semantics></math>.

keeping a phone in the bedroom and usual sleep, for the 300 students sampled
phones in the bedroom and less sleep, because phones keep students awake

options: Because 0.0165 < 0.05, reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.0165 > 0.05, fail to reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.0165 > 0.05, reject the null hypothesis.
Because 0.0165 < 0.05, accept the null hypothesis.

why.1: Check the inequality: the p-value 0.0165 is less than alpha 0.05, so reject the null hypothesis.

conclude.model: Because the p-value of 0.0165 is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. There is convincing evidence of an association between keeping a phone in the bedroom and usual hours of sleep for students at the school.
